title: Comparatives and Superlatives
summary: How to form and spell comparatives and superlatives, as...as, irregular forms, fewer or less, and why writers use them in persuasive texts, adverts and reviews.

blocks.text: A **comparative** compares **two** things (*taller than*). A **superlative** compares **three or more** and shows the top or bottom (*the tallest*).

items: Comparative: *The Nile is **longer than** the Thames.*
Superlative: *The Nile is **the longest** river in Africa.*

rows: one vowel + one consonant: big, hot, thin
the biggest, the hottest, the thinnest
the happiest, the busiest, the easiest
long (most two syllables, all three or more): careful, beautiful, dangerous
the most careful, the most dangerous
the best, the worst, the furthest/farthest

blocks.title: Remember the little words
blocks.text: Comparatives usually need **than**: *bigger **than** a bus*. Superlatives usually need **the**: ***the** biggest animal*.

items: With *as ... as* (the same): *My bag is **as heavy as** yours.*
With *not as ... as* (less): *The film was **not as exciting as** the book.*
Going down: *This puzzle is **less difficult than** the last one.* / *the **least** expensive ticket*
Adverbs too: *She ran **faster** than me. / He spoke **more quietly** than before.*
Getting stronger: *The storm grew **stronger and stronger**.* / *It became **more and more** frightening.*

blocks.text: 4. Fewer or less? Many or much?

blocks.title: Never double them
items: *more better* ✗ → *better* ✓
*the most fastest* ✗ → *the fastest* ✓
*more easier* ✗ → *easier* ✓
*badder* ✗ → *worse* ✓
*gooder / the goodest* ✗ → *better / the best* ✓
*bigger then* ✗ → *bigger **than*** ✓
*biger / hotest / happyer* ✗ → *bigger / hottest / happier* ✓ (spelling rules)

blocks.title: Reading questions in this style
items: *Find and copy a comparative adjective from the text.* (for example *bigger, more dangerous*)
*Find a superlative that the writer uses to persuade the reader.*
*Why does the writer use the superlative “the most exciting”?* → to make the place or product sound better than all the others and persuade the reader.

blocks.text: **Why do writers use comparatives and superlatives?** To compare things clearly, to show which is best or worst, to make something sound better than anything else in persuasive texts and adverts (*the most exciting ride in Egypt*), and to give a clear judgement in reviews.

rows: *Visit the **biggest** water park in Hurghada, with **longer** slides than ever before!*
*The second half of the book is **more gripping than** the first.*
*Walking to school is **cheaper** and **healthier than** going by car, but it is **slower**.*
*The cheetah is **the fastest** land animal in the world.*
*It was **the darkest** night of the year.*

blocks.title: نصيحة سريعة
items: الكلمة القصيرة تاخد er أو est، والطويلة تاخد more أو most. ما تجمعش الاتنين: more better غلط.
المقارنة بين حاجتين = er + than. الأفضل من الكل = the + est.
fewer مع الحاجات اللي بتتعد (fewer cars)، و less مع اللي ما بتتعدش (less water).

items.q: Correct: *This is the most best day of my life.*
items.a: *This is **the best** day of my life.*

items.q: Write the comparative of *busy* and the superlative of *thin*.
Correct: *There is less people here than yesterday.*
items.a: *There **are fewer** people here than yesterday.* (people are countable and plural)

items.q: Complete: *A plane is ______ (fast) than a train.*
Complete: *That was ______ (bad) film I have ever seen.*
Complete: *Science is ______ (interesting) than history for me.*
Correct: *My brother is more taller then me.*
Rewrite with *not as ... as*: *Alex is faster than Tarek.*
Why might a leaflet say *the friendliest hotel on the coast*?
items.a: The superlative makes the hotel sound better than every other hotel, which persuades the reader to choose it.

items.q: Choose: *There is (fewer / less) traffic on Fridays.*
